title: Perpetua and Felicity
hookLine: a young noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, face the arena together, and one reaches out a hand to lift the other

lines: ALL SHE HAS TO DO IS DENY IT.
cards: A father is on his knees in a prison in Carthage, in North Africa, begging his daughter. Have pity on my gray hair. Have pity on your mother, your brothers, your baby son, who won't live without you.
His daughter is Vibia Perpetua: well born, educated, a new mother nursing her child in a cell. She has been arrested as a Christian. All she has to do is say she isn't one.
And for a long stretch of the account, the words are Perpetua's own: her prison diary, in the first person, kept by the people who loved her.

teach.h: A WATER JUG: I AM WHAT I AM.
teach.b: Perpetua answers her father with a water jug. She points to one lying nearby: can that be called by any other name than what it is? No, he says.
So, she says, I can't call myself anything other than what I am, a Christian.

In prison with her is Felicity, an enslaved woman, heavily pregnant. Felicity's fear is a quiet one: that her pregnancy will hold back her execution, and she'll die later, without her friends, among common criminals.
The others pray with her, and she goes into labor in the prison. She gives birth to a daughter, and a Christian woman takes the baby to raise as her own.
Now there are two new mothers, one free and well born, one enslaved: nothing in common by the rules of their city, everything in common by the rules of their faith.
In the arena, the account says, a wild cow throws the two women down. Perpetua gets up first.

teach.h: SHE GAVE HER HAND AND LIFTED HER UP.
teach.b: She sees Felicity on the ground, goes to her, gives her her hand, and lifts her up, and the two stand together. Before the end, the martyrs give one another the kiss of peace.

Churches that remember them still name them side by side, the noblewoman and the slave. Some readers notice the small things the account keeps: a jug, a father's gray hair, a woman pinning up her hair in the arena.
It reads less like a legend about saints than a diary about people.

how: Christians who keep a calendar of saints remember Perpetua and Felicity together, on one day, and their story is sometimes read or preached then.

games.q: you're Perpetua. your father is on his knees, begging you to deny you're a Christian. your baby is in your arms. what do you say?
o: say what he wants, and keep your faith quietly.
point to a water jug: it can't be called anything else.
say nothing, and let the judge decide.
games.why: she points to the jug. it can only be called what it is, and so can she: a Christian.

practice: If someone is beside you, take their hand for this minute, without needing to explain.
If you're alone, rest one hand in the other, bring to mind someone who's been knocked down lately, and picture going to them and lifting them up.
If you pray, hold them in prayer; if not, hold the picture of the two of you standing together.

wordCard.voice: Christiana sum. The Latin answer Perpetua gave at her hearing, naming herself a Christian. She and Felicity, a noblewoman and an enslaved woman, both new mothers, are remembered side by side.
